prompt: A team switches off a noisy scanner, and the next report shows 30% fewer findings. What does the count of findings say about the team's security?

choices.text: It improved by about the same 30%
choices.why: The code did not change. Fewer findings came from looking less, which is the opposite of an improvement.

choices.text: Nothing, on its own
choices.why: Right. The count fell because less is being looked at; it moves the same way for opposite reasons, so it needs coverage beside it.

choices.text: It got worse by about 30%
choices.why: A drop in findings is not a rise in risk by the same amount; the count cannot say how much risk there is.

choices.text: The scanner had been raising false positives
choices.why: Maybe, but the count cannot tell; a noisy scanner also finds real things.

prompt: Match each number to what it cannot see.

pairs.right: whether the SLA itself is sensible

right_distractors: how many developers the team has

prompt: Which date should a finding's age be counted from?

choices.text: The day somebody triaged it
choices.why: That hides the time it sat unread, which is part of what is being measured.

choices.text: The day a ticket was opened for it
choices.why: A ticket is a step after triage, so it hides the same wait.

choices.text: The day a check first raised it
choices.why: Right. The pipeline's logs record it, and every day after it counts.

choices.text: The day of the release whose code contained it
choices.why: The release date is not when anybody knew about it, and many findings are in code never released.

prompt: Why does gen.py create its generator with random.Random(19) instead of using random's default state?

choices.text: Seed 19 gives a more realistic distribution
choices.why: Any seed gives the same distribution; the number only fixes which draws come out.

choices.text: So your numbers match the lesson's
choices.why: Right. Every run writes the same files: two runs gave the same checksums, which is what makes the data set quotable.

choices.text: The default state is not random enough for statistics
choices.why: The default is fine for statistics; the problem is that it differs on every run.

choices.text: Python refuses lognormvariate without a seed
choices.why: It does not; it would simply draw different numbers each time.

prompt: In the generated findings, how many closed findings left the list without being fixed (closed as "won't fix" or as false positives)?
Why does the generator need an inventory at all, when the measurements are about findings?

choices.text: To give each finding a team
choices.why: The team could be a column of the findings alone; that is not what the inventory adds.

choices.text: Because a CSV join needs a second file to join against
choices.why: Nothing about CSV requires a second file.

choices.text: To set how many findings each scanner raises
choices.why: The rates are in RATE; the inventory says which scanners run where.

choices.text: Unscanned targets produce no rows
choices.why: Right. Only the inventory can show what is missing from the findings.

prompt: For medium findings the mean time to fix is 47.3 days and the median 34.5. What does the gap say?

choices.text: A few slow fixes pulled the mean above the typical one
choices.why: Right. That is the long tail; the 90th percentile, 103 days, measures it.

choices.text: Half the fixes took more than 47.3 days
choices.why: Half took more than the median, 34.5; that is what a median is.

choices.text: The data set has an error in how it was generated
choices.why: Mean above median is what fix times look like, not a fault in the data.

choices.text: Most fixes took between 34.5 and 47.3 days
choices.why: The two numbers are not a range; most fixes took less than 40 days.

prompt: One medium fix took 199 days. If it had taken 400, what would change in the ttr report's medium row?

choices.text: The median would rise by about a day and a half
choices.why: The median is the middle value; moving the largest one does not move the middle.

choices.text: Only the mean, by about a day and a half; the median stays
choices.why: Right: 201 extra days over 134 fixes, and the middle value stays where it was.

choices.text: Neither: one finding among 134 is too few to matter
choices.why: It is too few for the median and not for the mean, which adds every value.

choices.text: The 90th percentile would roughly double, to about 200 days
choices.why: The p90 is a rank, the value at 90% of the way; the largest value is above it.

prompt: A team fixes its quick findings and leaves the hard ones open. Month after month, its median time to remediate improves. Why?

choices.text: The hard ones are still open, so they are not in its input
choices.why: Right. The report counts only fixed findings: survivorship bias. The debt report is where those findings show.

choices.text: Quick findings have a shorter SLA
choices.why: The SLA depends on severity, not on how quick a fix is.

choices.text: The median ignores findings older than the SLA
choices.why: The median ignores nothing that is in its input; the open ones are simply not in it.

choices.text: Hard findings are closed as false positives
choices.why: Nothing in the scenario closes them; they stay open.

prompt: Which of these come out of an SLA per severity? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: The share of fixes that landed within the promised days
choices.why: Right. It is the last column of the ttr report.

choices.text: The open findings already past the promised days
choices.why: Right. The debt report counts them: 2 high, 9 medium and 7 low.

choices.text: The severity each finding deserves
choices.why: Severity comes first; the SLA is looked up from it.

choices.text: Whether the SLA itself is sensible
choices.why: No number computed against the SLA can judge the SLA; people agree on it.

prompt: In the generated inventory, how many targets (repositories and images together) have no scanner at all?
web-assets has 3 findings and storefront has 57. What can you conclude about web-assets?

choices.text: Its code is safer than storefront's
choices.why: Only the secret scanner looks at it, so most kinds of finding cannot appear there.

choices.text: Its team fixes findings faster
choices.why: The count of findings says nothing about speed; time to remediate does.

choices.text: Little: only one scanner of the four looks at it
choices.why: Right. The coverage report shows it, and the count of findings cannot.

choices.text: It has been archived and is no longer developed
choices.why: Nothing in the data says so; it is in the inventory with one scanner.

prompt: A coverage report says 100% of repositories run the dependency scanner. Which situation would still make that number overstate what is known?

choices.text: Some repositories may have two scanners
choices.why: More scanners on a target do not make its coverage of one scanner false.

choices.text: Its job is allowed to fail and nobody reads it
choices.why: Right. It runs as a job allowed to fail: configured is not the same as deciding anything, so it counts as covered while nobody is told.

choices.text: The scanner found zero findings in half of them
choices.why: Zero findings is a result, unless the scanner had nothing to read; the count alone does not overstate.

choices.text: The repositories are in different languages
choices.why: Language matters to which scanner applies, not to whether the one that runs is counted honestly.

prompt: Why does the debt report split open findings into age buckets instead of reporting their average age?

choices.text: An average hides the shape
choices.why: Right. An average moves as much for one very old fix as for many new ones; a growing 181+ column is the pattern to catch, and buckets keep it visible.

choices.text: Buckets are easier to compute
choices.why: The average is one line of code; ease is not the argument.

choices.text: The SLA is defined in buckets
choices.why: The SLA is a number of days per severity, compared separately in the last column.

choices.text: Ages of open findings cannot be averaged
choices.why: They can; the result is simply a poor summary.

prompt: A quarterly trend where the open count holds flat means the team closes about as many findings as it opens: it keeps up, but the ___ findings stay where they are.
Next quarter the open count falls from 60 to 35 while findings closed per quarter stay near 126. What should be checked first?

choices.text: Whether the SLA was shortened
choices.why: A shorter SLA changes what is late, not how many are open.

choices.text: Whether the teams got faster
choices.why: Closing stayed the same, so speed is not what moved.

choices.text: Whether the median time to remediate fell over the quarter
choices.why: The median of fixed findings cannot explain a fall in open ones when closing is flat.

choices.text: Whether a scanner was switched off
choices.why: Right, or a target left the inventory: coverage first. Closing held, so fewer opened, and the first suspect is less being looked at.

prompt: payments has the best median days to close, 7, and closed the most findings, 135. What does the wont_fix column add?

choices.text: That payments has fewer findings to fix
choices.why: It has as many as anybody; it closed 135, the most.

choices.text: That 41% of its closures were not fixes
choices.why: Right. Of 135 closed, 71 were fixed; the rest left the list in days without a fix.

choices.text: That payments marks more false positives
choices.why: False positives are counted apart from wont_fix.

choices.text: Nothing: wont_fix is a legitimate resolution
choices.why: It is legitimate one finding at a time, and the share is still what explains the median.

prompt: ttr-any counts every route off the list as a remediation. What happens to the medium median, and why?

choices.text: It rises, because more findings are counted
choices.why: More findings counted does not mean longer ones; these were closed fast.

choices.text: It stays the same, because the fixes did not change
choices.why: The fixes did not change, and the median did anyway: the input changed.

choices.text: It falls to 22, because closures that were not fixes now count
choices.why: Right, from 34.5: 61 findings closed without a fix join the count. Nothing was fixed faster; only the filter moved.

choices.text: It falls, because false positives are fixed faster
choices.why: A false positive is not fixed at all; it is closed.

prompt: Leadership wants one number to judge teams next year and proposes median days to close. Which change keeps the number honest?

choices.text: Report it only for critical findings
choices.why: Critical findings can be downgraded too, and the median still ignores open ones.

choices.text: Use the mean instead of the median
choices.why: The mean is moved by a few slow fixes and is gamed by the same closures.

choices.text: Pair it with the won't-fix share
choices.why: Right, and count only fixed findings. A pair that pulls against each other shows gaming on the same page, and fixed-only stops the filter trick.

choices.text: Tie a bonus to it, so teams take it seriously
choices.why: That is the arrangement in which a measure stops measuring.

prompt: Put the steps of turning a year of scanner output into a report in order.
items: decide what one finding is, and merge duplicates
record each finding's opening date, closing date and resolution
list every target that exists, scanned or not
compute time to remediate, debt and coverage
report them in pairs that pull against each other

prompt: Whoever answers for risk asks for one slide. Which pair of numbers belongs on it?

choices.text: Findings found this quarter, and findings closed
choices.why: That says how busy the scanners and teams were, not what is unknown or late.

choices.text: Coverage per scanner, and the debt past SLA by severity
choices.why: Right. How much is unknown, and how much was promised and not done.

choices.text: The median time to remediate per team
choices.why: That is the engineering lead's view, and on its own it is the easiest to game.

choices.text: The open list sorted by age
choices.why: That is the team's work list, too detailed for this reader.
